title: Design a Notification System
summary: You'll be able to design a push/email/SMS notification platform with queues per channel and priority, user preferences and quiet hours, retries, deduplication and rate limits, sized from a campaign burst.

questions.prompt: Why should the notification API put requests on a **queue** and return `202 Accepted`, instead of calling APNs, SES or Twilio directly and returning `200` when the message is delivered?
questions.hint: Think about a slow provider, a burst of 100M messages, and the service that called you.
keyPoints: Providers are slow or unavailable at times; a synchronous call would make every producer wait or fail with them
A queue absorbs bursts (e.g. a campaign) so workers can drain at a sustainable, rate-limited pace
Queues decouple and isolate channels: an SMS outage doesn't block push or email
Failed sends can be retried with backoff from the queue without the caller retrying
202 means accepted for processing, not delivered; status is tracked separately
questions.answer:
Because the slow, unreliable part (the provider) should never be in the caller's request path.

- **Providers are sometimes slow or down.** If the API called Twilio synchronously and Twilio took 10 s or failed, every producer (order service, login service) would hang or fail with it.
- **Queues absorb bursts.** A marketing campaign to 100M users in an hour is ~27,800 sends/s. The API just enqueues; workers drain at a pace that respects each provider's rate limit.
- **Isolation.** With per-channel queues, an SMS outage only makes SMS messages wait; push and email keep flowing.
- **Retries belong to the system.** A failed send is retried from the queue with exponential backoff, so the caller doesn't need its own retry logic (which would also create duplicates).

`202 Accepted` honestly means "**accepted for processing**, not yet delivered". Delivery may take seconds or, for a campaign, an hour, and it might bounce. Callers who care can check status separately, e.g. `GET /v1/notifications/{id}` or delivery webhooks.

questions.prompt:
Marketing wants to send a push to **60 million** users within **30 minutes**, and an SMS to the **2 million** who have no app installed. One push provider call takes **80 ms**; one worker process can keep **200** calls in flight. SMS costs **$0.008** each.

Estimate the push rate, in-flight calls, number of push worker processes, and the SMS bill.
keyPoints: Push rate = 60M / 1,800 s ≈ 33,300 pushes/s
In flight = 33,300 × 0.08 s ≈ 2,670 concurrent calls
Workers = 2,670 / 200 ≈ 14, so ~15–20 with headroom
SMS cost = 2M × $0.008 = $16,000 for the campaign
Notes that provider rate limits, not your workers, may be the real cap, and the campaign must not starve transactional traffic

questions.prompt: Users report getting the same "Your order has shipped" push **three times**. List the places in the pipeline where duplicates can be created, and the fix for each.
questions.hint: Follow the message from the order service to the phone and ask "who retries here?" at each hop.
keyPoints: The producer retried its API call after a timeout: fix with an Idempotency-Key (e.g. order-81723-shipped) checked with SET NX / unique index at intake
A worker crashed or timed out after sending but before acking, so the queue redelivered: record per-notification-per-channel send state before/after the provider call and check it on redelivery
The worker retried the provider after a timeout even though the provider had sent: use provider idempotency features where available and accept a small residual risk
Multiple registered tokens for the same device (reinstall) can also cause duplicates: dedupe device tokens and remove invalid ones
States that end-to-end delivery is at-least-once, so dedup must happen at each hop
questions.answer:
Walk the message hop by hop and ask "who retries here?". Delivery is **at-least-once** end to end, so each hop needs its own dedup.

| Where | How the duplicate happens | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Producer → API | The order service timed out and retried `POST /notifications`; both requests were accepted | Send an **Idempotency-Key** like `order-81723-shipped`; intake does `SET key NX` in Redis or relies on a unique index, and returns the original `notificationId` on a repeat |
| Queue → worker | The worker sent the push, then crashed (or timed out) before **acking**; the queue redelivered | Record per-notification-per-channel state (`n_9f2/push: attempting` → `sent`) before and after the provider call; on redelivery, skip if `sent` |
| Worker → provider | The APNs call timed out, the worker retried, but APNs had actually delivered | Use provider idempotency features where they exist (e.g. a collapse ID for push); otherwise accept a small residual risk |
| Device tokens | The user reinstalled the app, so two valid tokens point at the same phone | Dedupe tokens per device ID, and delete tokens the provider reports invalid (e.g. `410`) |

Three copies suggests two of these hops misfired, e.g. a producer retry plus a redelivery.

questions.prompt: Write `canSend(history, now, limit, windowMs)` for a per-user frequency cap. `history` is an array of timestamps (ms) of previous marketing sends for this user. Return `true` if fewer than `limit` sends happened in the last `windowMs` milliseconds (a sliding window), and if so record `now` in `history`. Also drop timestamps that are too old so the array doesn't grow forever.
questions.hint: Filter out entries `<= now - windowMs`, then compare the remaining count to the limit.
keyPoints: Removes timestamps older than now - windowMs (mutating or returning a pruned list)
Counts only sends inside the sliding window
Returns false without recording when the count is already >= limit
Returns true and appends now when allowed
Correct boundary handling (a send exactly windowMs ago has expired)

questions.prompt: A 100M-user marketing blast starts at 10:00. At 10:05 a user asks for a login **one-time passcode** and it arrives at 10:52. Redesign the pipeline so this can't happen.
questions.hint: Where was the OTP waiting? Think queues, workers and provider quotas.
keyPoints: The OTP waited in the same FIFO queue behind millions of marketing messages
Separate queues (topics) per priority: critical (OTP/security), transactional, bulk
Dedicated or reserved worker capacity for critical lanes so bulk can't consume all workers
Reserve or separate provider quota (rate limit budget, possibly a separate sender/account) for critical messages
Throttle the campaign producer (feed batches gradually) and monitor queue age/latency per lane with alerts
questions.answer:
**What went wrong:** the OTP went into the **same FIFO queue** as 100M marketing messages. At ~28k sends/s the blast takes about an hour, so the passcode waited behind millions of flyers.

**Redesign**
1. **Priority lanes.** Separate queues (topics) per priority: **critical** (OTP, security alerts), **transactional** (order updates), **bulk** (marketing). Category decides the lane.
2. **Reserved workers.** Each lane has its own worker pool (or workers consume critical strictly first), so bulk can never take every worker. The critical pool is small but always idle-ready.
3. **Reserved provider quota.** If the SMS account allows 1,000 msg/s, reserve e.g. 200/s for critical traffic, or use a separate sender ID/account for OTPs, so the campaign can't trigger `429`s that block passcodes.
4. **Throttle the campaign producer.** Feed the blast in batches (e.g. 1,000 users at a time) at a controlled rate instead of dumping 100M messages at 10:00.
5. **Monitor per lane.** Track queue age and send latency per lane, with an alert such as "critical p99 > 10 s".

Result: an OTP requested at 10:05 is sent within seconds, while the campaign still finishes within its hour.

questions.prompt: The order service does `UPDATE orders SET status='shipped'` and then calls `POST /v1/notifications`. Occasionally customers never get the "shipped" email, and occasionally they get it for an order whose update was rolled back. Fix this end to end.
questions.hint: Day 44: you can't atomically write to a database and call another service, but you can write two rows in one transaction.
keyPoints: The DB write and the API call are not atomic: a crash between them loses the notification; calling before commit can notify for a rolled-back change
Transactional outbox: insert an outbox row (event + idempotency key) in the same DB transaction as the order update
A relay (poller or change-data-capture) publishes outbox rows to the notification queue/API, retrying until acknowledged, then marks them sent
Delivery from the outbox is at-least-once, so a stable idempotency key (e.g. order-<id>-shipped) dedups at intake
Result: notified if and only if the update committed, with no duplicates visible to the user
questions.answer:
**The bug:** the database update and the API call are not **atomic** (all-or-nothing together).
- Update commits, then the service crashes before calling the API → no email ever.
- Call the API before or inside the transaction, then the transaction rolls back → email for a change that never happened.

**Fix: the transactional outbox.**
1. In the **same transaction** as the order update, insert an `outbox` row:
```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 81723;
INSERT INTO outbox (event, payload, idempotency_key)
VALUES ('order_shipped', '{"orderId":81723}', 'order-81723-shipped');
COMMIT;
```
Both rows commit or neither does.
2. A **relay** (a poller reading unsent outbox rows, or change data capture from the DB log) calls `POST /v1/notifications` or publishes to the queue, **retrying until acknowledged**, then marks the row sent.
3. The relay can crash after sending but before marking, so delivery is **at-least-once**. The stable key `order-81723-shipped` makes intake dedupe the repeat.

**Result:** a notification is sent **if and only if** the update committed, and the user sees it once.
